study.title: Does the wording of a question change what witnesses remember?

study.introduction: Researchers tested the misinformation effect: the idea that misleading information given after an event can change a person's memory of it. They predicted that a question suggesting a detail that was not there would lead more people to later report seeing that detail.
study.participants: 120 adults (ages 18 to 64, 62 women and 58 men) recruited from a public library and a community college in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Most (85%) had a high school diploma; 40% were current college students. The study was approved by the college's institutional review board. Each participant signed an informed consent form stating they would watch a video of a minor robbery and could stop at any time.
study.method: Each participant watched the same two-minute video of a man taking a woman's bag at a bus stop. A computer randomly assigned each participant to one of two groups of 60. Right after the video, both groups answered 10 written questions about it. For the misleading group, one question was "Did the man put the bag under his red jacket before he ran?" For the neutral group, the same question read "Did the man put the bag under his jacket before he ran?" In the video the jacket was gray. Forty-eight hours later, participants returned and, without seeing the video again, rated how sure they were that the man wore a red jacket, from 1 (definitely not) to 7 (definitely yes).
study.results: The misleading group's mean rating was 4.6 (SD = 1.5); the neutral group's mean rating was 2.1 (SD = 1.2). The difference was statistically significant, p < .01. The effect size was large.
study.discussion: At the end of the second session, each participant was told that the jacket was gray and that one question had been worded to mislead. The researchers concluded that a single misleading word can change what people later remember.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.point: Identifies the method as an experiment (the question wording was manipulated and participants were randomly assigned). A correlational study, a survey, naturalistic observation, a case study, a hybrid, or several methods listed does not earn the point.

parts.sample: This study is an experiment, because the researchers manipulated the wording of the question and randomly assigned participants to the misleading or neutral group.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: State the operational definition of memory for the jacket's color.

rubric.point: States that memory for the jacket's color was measured as each participant's rating, 48 hours later, of how sure they were the man wore a red jacket on a 1 (definitely not) to 7 (definitely yes) scale. A general definition of memory or of the misinformation effect, or "a rating" with no scale or no content, does not earn the point.
accept: the 1-to-7 rating of certainty that the jacket was red, made 48 hours after the video
how sure participants were, from 1 to 7, that the man wore a red jacket, two days later

parts.sample: Memory for the jacket's color was operationally defined as each participant's rating, 48 hours after the video, of how sure they were that the man wore a red jacket, on a scale from 1 (definitely not) to 7 (definitely yes).

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe what the difference between the group means, and its statistical significance, shows.

rubric.point: Describes that the misleading group was more sure the jacket was red (4.6 versus 2.1 on the 7-point scale) and that, because the difference is statistically significant, it is unlikely to be due to chance. Restating the numbers without saying what they show, reversing the direction, or defining "mean" or "significant" in general does not earn the point.
accept: the misleading group rated a red jacket as more likely, and the difference is unlikely to be due to chance
people asked about a "red jacket" were about 2.5 points more sure it was red, more than chance would explain

parts.sample: The misleading group was much more sure that the jacket was red (a mean of 4.6, above the scale's middle) than the neutral group (2.1, close to "definitely not"). Because the difference is statistically significant, a gap this large is unlikely to be due to chance differences between the groups, so the misleading word, not chance, likely made people more confident in a false detail.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the researchers followed, as the summary describes it, and explain how the researchers applied it.

rubric.point: Identifies a safeguard the summary describes (IRB approval, informed consent, the right to withdraw, or debriefing) and explains how it was applied in this study. A guideline the summary does not mention (such as confidentiality), or a design feature such as random assignment, does not earn the point.
accept: debriefing: at the end of the second session participants were told the jacket was gray and one question was meant to mislead
informed consent: each participant signed a form saying they would watch a video of a minor robbery and could stop at any time
IRB approval: the college's institutional review board approved the study before it began
the right to withdraw: the consent form told participants they could stop at any time

parts.sample: The researchers used debriefing. Because one question was worded to mislead, at the end of the second session they told each participant that the jacket was really gray and that the question had been designed to mislead them.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain whether the results of this study can be generalized to high school students who witness a crime.

rubric.point: Makes a claim (yes, no or partly) about generalizing to high school students and supports it with specific characteristics of the participants (age 18 to 64, adults from a library and community college in Minneapolis, 40% college students). "Partly" needs a reason on each side. Arguments from sample size alone, random assignment, or design flaws do not earn the point.
accept: partly: participants were adults 18-64, older than high school students, though 40% were students
no: no participant was under 18, and they were recruited at a library and a college in one city

parts.sample: The results can only partly be generalized to high school students. On one hand, 40% of the participants were current college students, close in age and setting to older high school students. On the other hand, no participant was younger than 18, the age range ran up to 64, and all were recruited in one city, so younger teens who see a real crime may respond differently to a misleading question.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain how the results of the study support or refute the hypothesis that misleading information after an event changes memory of the event. Use specific results from the study.

rubric.point: States that the results support the hypothesis and cites a specific, accurate result (the misleading group's mean certainty of 4.6 versus 2.1 for the neutral group, or a statistically significant difference).
accept: support: the misleading group rated 4.6 and the neutral group 2.1
the significant difference in certainty that the jacket was red supports it

rubric.point: Explains how that result shows memory was changed: the only difference between the groups was the word "red", given after the video, and 48 hours later that group was more sure of a detail they never saw, so post-event information was blended into the memory (the misinformation effect). Restating the result, or saying it "proves" the hypothesis, does not earn the point.
accept: because the groups differed only in the word "red" after the event, the higher certainty shows the misleading word was added to the memory
the false detail came from the question, not the video, so information after the event changed what people remembered

parts.sample: The results support the hypothesis. Two days later, the misleading group was much more sure the man wore a red jacket (mean 4.6) than the neutral group (mean 2.1), and the difference was statistically significant. Because both groups saw the identical video and were randomly assigned, the only difference was the word "red" in a question asked after the event. People in that group became more confident of a detail that was never in the video, which shows that misleading information after an event was blended into their memory of it: the misinformation effect.
